What's moving the market: Singapore's biggest property deals and hottest searches (Sept 25)
article:
Here is this week’s data-led look at Singapore’s property market, covering record transactions, rental benchmarks and the most searched homes on EdgeProp.

The following insights are compiled from EdgeProp Buddy , URA Realis and data.gov.sg, downloaded as of Sept 22.

Non-landed private homes — new launches, resales and rents

The highest-priced condo unit recorded over the last fortnight was at luxury District 10 development Ardmore Park , when a ninth-floor apartment was sold for $12.55 million on Sept 8.

Next was a Skywaters Residences unit on the 28th storey which went for $11.48 million ($5,498 psf). It is part of the residential component of 63-storey mixed-use development The Skywaters on Shenton Way, set to be Singapore’s tallest building when it is completed.

In the leasing market, the most popular rented condo in the Core Central Region (CCR), based on latest available data for contracts starting in August 2026, was D’Leedon with 55 deals. The 99-year leasehold project in prime District 10 houses 1,703 condo units and 12 landed units.

The next most popular rented CCR condos was The Sail @ Marina Bay with 39 rental transactions, and Marina One Residences with 38.

The Boulevard Residence was in pole position among CCR units with the highest rents, with an apartment commanding $41,000 per month. Measuring more than 7,000 sq ft, the unit has five bedrooms, with its lease starting this August. The Boulevard Residence is a freehold 45-unit apartment complex on Cuscaden Walk.

Following closely on the list was a Cape Royale unit fetching $40,000 in monthly rent. Located on Cove Way in Sentosa Cove , the 302-unit Cape Royale condo has posted an average rental price of $5.9 psf per month, based on URA rental data in the last 12 months.

Landed homes — highest transacted prices and rents

A semi-detached house on Mount Sinai Avenue was sold for nearly $12.3 million ($2,233), making it the most expensive landed property transacted in the last 14 days. It sits on 5,504 sq ft of land with a 999-year leasehold tenure.

Meanwhile, a Sian Tuan Avenue house fetched $10.93 million, while a Jalan Raya property went for $7.5 million.

HDB flats — top prices and rents, most transacted blocks

A five-room flat on levels 28 to 30 at Pinnacle@Duxton on Cantonment Road, transacted for $1.701 million, was the highest-priced HDB unit sold during the period in review. It also broke the price record at the development.

The flat’s owners told EdgeProp Singapore that the outcome came as a surprise to them, as the unit was not on the highest floors and was also largely unrenovated.

Meanwhile, a five-room flat at Block 273A Bishan Street 24 , on the 31st to 33rd storeys, changed hands for $1.6 million. It is part of Natura Loft , a popular Design, Build and Sell Scheme (DBSS) public housing project.

title: Elevate Capital gives 30-year-old Stamford Court a new lease of life as Stamford Place
article:
For the past two decades, Singapore Management University (SMU) students crossed Stamford Road to Stamford Court mainly for two reasons: the bus stop in front of the building, or the 24-hour Cheers convenience store at the corner of the four-storey commercial building with the clock tower.

“The whole area was quite dead,” says Randy Chan, principal architect at Zarch Collaboratives, which led the transformation of the former Stamford Court, now Stamford Place .

Elevate Capital, which targets well-located buildings that are 20 to 30 years old and undermanaged, acquired Stamford Court with joint-venture partner PGIM Real Estate for $132 million in October 2024. It sits on a 99-year lease from 1994, with about 67 years remaining.

Search for the latest New Launches , to find out the transaction prices and available units

“We felt that it was a high-quality asset — very central, great location, but trapped in time,” says Ashish Manchharam, founder and managing partner of Elevate Capital.

“We saw the opportunity to reposition the property to cater to the students, those working in the neighbouring office buildings, tourists and also guests from the nearby hotels,” he adds.

Manchharam hopes that the refreshed Stamford Place will be “the catalyst for the area”.

Completed in 1996, Stamford Court had reached the age when many owners begin to weigh tearing down and rebuilding. Instead, its structure was retained, and its granite cladding and clock tower reworked rather than replaced.

To cater to the neighbourhood, a variety of F&B options were introduced in the ground-floor units. They include Blue Label Tavern, which has already opened. It will soon be joined by Gelato Messina, which will host a pop-up by cookie bakeshop Butter, as well as Japanese restaurant Yoruya and Nanyang Old Coffee.

Complementing these is Stamford Social, a 50-seat all-day European-inspired café and bar connected to the lobby of the new Stamford Place. “We need to have a variety of affordable, all-day F&B options to cater to the neighbourhood,” he says.

The ground floor will also house a wellness concept and Cold Storage On The Go, the supermarket chain’s new small-format store.

The three upper floors now house a co-working space run by The Great Room and 66 serviced apartments under a new serviced apartment brand, APT, created by Elevate Capital.

Even before Stamford Place fully opens, early indications suggest strong demand, with The Great Room co-working space continuing to be filled. APT has already secured long-term bookings. Given its proximity to the track, it has also taken week-long stays for the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix 2026 from Oct 9 to 11, notes Manchharam.

Updating for modern-day use

Zarch worked alongside the Ministry of Design (MOD), whose founder and director of design, Colin Seah, led the design of the exterior refresh and the interiors.

For Zarch, the main challenge during the refurbishment was converting the former office building into a mixed-use development with serviced apartments. Bathrooms had to be fitted in every unit across all floors, and approvals had to be obtained from various government agencies before work could start.

As a result, construction began only in October 2025 and was completed at the end of August. The entire interior was gutted, leaving only the lift core and the building’s structural shell, says Chan.

The building’s reddish-brown granite cladding, similar in tone to Ngee Ann City ’s, was unmistakably of the 1990s. Removing it, however, risked damaging the waterproofing and windows, says MOD’s Seah. Instead, façade specialist Building Façade Group applied a textured, stone-effect coating over the existing granite, giving the building a lighter grey finish.

“We wanted the façade to be stately, akin to our neighbours,” says Seah. He is referring to the historic buildings of the Civic District around Stamford Place.  Among them are the Vanguard Building, Stamford House (now part of The Capitol Kempinski Hotel) and the Peranakan Museum.

The Vanguard Building and Stamford House were both designed by Regent Alfred John Bidwell, one of Singapore’s most influential colonial-era architects. Bidwell is best known for Raffles Hotel and the Victoria Memorial Hall (now Victoria Concert Hall).

At Stamford Place, the most prominent feature is the clock tower, which Zarch renovated. “We cleaned up the clock, gave it a new mechanism, and it now has a new lease of life,” says Chan.

The main entrance has also been repositioned, says MOD’s Seah. Designed as “a layered arched portal”, it now sits directly beneath the clock tower as the building’s focal point. Previously, that spot was occupied by Cheers, while the main entrance was tucked away at the side, “which was very odd”, he adds.

Both Zarch and MOD had worked with Manchharam when he led real estate investment firm 8M Real Estate. MOD had designed the interiors of the conservation shophouse at 28 Stanley Street. Meanwhile, Zarch worked on several adaptive reuse projects involving conservation properties, including the former Eu Yan Sang Building on South Bridge Road and conservation shophouses at 111 Jalan Besar as well as Tanjong Pagar.

Of time and place

Stamford Place’s site has a long history. The corner of Stamford Road and Hill Street was once occupied by Eu Court, built in the late 1920s by businessman Eu Tong Sen. It was demolished in 1992 to make way for road widening works along Hill Street and Victoria Street. Singapore Land Group acquired the site in 1994 and completed Stamford Court two years later.

While the exterior of Stamford Place is now light grey, the interior palette is terracotta, reminiscent of the roof, floor and veranda tiles of the black-and-white bungalows designed by Bidwell, says Seah. “The whole spirit of the brand — APT and The Great Room — is about celebrating the human scale, and being warm and welcoming.”

The clock tower also inspired a theme of time that runs through the interiors. It is reflected in the horology-inspired LED chandelier in the lobby, and in the hourglass patterns on the upholstered leather panels lining the bar counters at Stamford Social, the concierge reception and The Great Room’s drawing room. “Once we nailed down the narrative with everyone, it became the North Star of the project,” says Seah.

Artworks by Singapore-based artists follow the theme. The common areas will feature works by Richard Hassell, co-founder of architecture firm Woha and an artist focused on textiles, rugs and three-dimensional architectural installations; Samuel Xun, known for his ornate sculptures, installations and textile compositions; and artist, designer and ceramicist Genevieve Ang. Meanwhile, the serviced apartments will display prints by visual artists and muralists, including Soph O and Bblob.

Work and stay under one roof

The Great Room by Industrious has taken about 30,000 sq ft across all of Level 2 and half of Level 3. Since The Great Room was acquired by US flexible workplace provider Industrious in May 2022, its other locations have been rebranded under the Industrious name.

However, The Great Room name was retained for Stamford Place as “it resonated with the overall building concept in terms of positioning”, says Manchharam. It is therefore positioned as “a white label brand”, similar to APT.

He expects occupancy at The Great Room to stabilise at about 90% by early 2027.

The APT serviced apartments occupy half of Level 3 and the entire Level 4. The 66 apartments are managed in partnership with Frasers Hospitality.

Rather than a corporate-style offering, APT is positioned as “an upscale serviced apartment with a boutique-hotel feel”, says Manchharam.

The surrounding area already has plenty of hotel rooms, he adds. Across Stamford Road are the 350-room Pullman and The Capitol Kempinski, with 155 rooms and suites. The 940-room Carlton Hotel Singapore is on Bras Basah Road, while further down at Funan , co-living property Lyf Funan has 329 units.

APT, however, is aimed primarily at guests with a minimum stay of a week. “We want to provide a space for those who want to stay longer, and therefore prefer to have home-like amenities,” says Manchharam.

Units range from studios to suites, with sizes averaging 35 sqm (377 sq ft). There are also dual-key units of about 50 sq m (538 sq ft), which include a common vestibule with a seating area, a pantry with a microwave oven, and a minibar refrigerator. These dual-key units cater to families.

The rooms have high ceilings and full-height windows, now fitted with a second layer of glass to reduce noise and glare. The walls and ceilings have also been acoustically treated. “We want to ensure that people can have a good night’s sleep,” says Manchharam.

Promotional rates are said to start at $268 per night, and are expected to stabilise closer to $300 for the entry-level studios, he adds. The expectation is that occupancy rates will stabilise at the “mid-80%” by early 2027.

APT guests share a gym on Level 3 with The Great Room’s members. They can also use its drawing room and book its meeting rooms.

“We wanted to have a more dynamic building; that’s why we wanted The Great Room and APT spaces to be integrated, so it feels more like a live, work, play environment,” says Manchharam.

Wider catchment

With 500 desks and 66 apartments, the building will accommodate 500 to 600 people when fully occupied, Manchharam estimates. The F&B outlets, however, are intended to draw not only Stamford Place’s occupiers but also people within a 50m to 100m radius — what he calls “our primary catchment”.

That includes SMU, which has more than 13,000 undergraduates, postgraduates and researchers, as well as guests at The Capitol Kempinski and Pullman. Furen International School will be taking over the neighbouring Vanguard Building as its new campus, while Sembcorp Industries’ headquarters is nearby at 30 Hill Street.

Just behind Stamford Place, the pedestrianised Armenian Street and the Peranakan Museum draw tourists, while Fort Canning Park is a short walk away.

Both Manchharam and Zarch’s Chan have tried out APT for themselves. Chan stayed over a weekend with his family. “We were tourists for a day,” he says. “The location is wonderful — you can walk to Raffles City, the museums, and even catch the light show during the Singapore Night Festival.”

During his stay, Manchharam went for a 7am run past Armenian Street, looping through Fort Canning Park and back.

Longer stays help serviced apartment guests get to know the area, says Chan. “When you have people staying for two to four weeks, they will start to understand and explore the neighbourhood.”

Tenant curation at Stamford Place has focused on operators already established in Singapore. “We wanted tenants with a track record for quality and the ability to bring people back as well,” says Manchharam. “The pricing also has to be managed, so it’s affordable for everyone.”

The Blue Label Tavern is a casual dining concept by Travis Masiero Restaurant Group, best known for Luke’s Oyster Bar and Chophouse. It specialises in stone-fired pizzas, dry-rubbed rotisserie chicken and beer on tap. Happy hour runs until 6pm, while the restaurant stays open until 10.30pm from Mondays to Saturdays. “Students from across the street can come here to grab a beer and dinner after class,” says Manchharam.

Manchharam lunches at Blue Label Tavern regularly and has run into groups from the National Gallery and Sembcorp, as well as SMU lecturers and families with young children. “It is a wide mix, and gives you an idea of the type of people who are in the area as well,” he says.

Stamford Social, meanwhile, is targeting the breakfast-to-evening crowd, operating as a café in the morning before switching to happy hour later in the day.

Merchant House

Elevate Capital’s second repositioning play is 51 Merchant Road, which it acquired jointly with LaSalle Investment Management for $121.8 million in February 2026, below the property’s market valuation of $152.7 million. Formerly occupied by Raffles Education, the four-storey building will be renamed Merchant House.

Omnicom has signed a five-year lease, with an option to renew, for 50,000 sq ft across the upper floors and the two adjoining rows of conservation shophouses fronting Fisher Street.

Manchharam plans to convert the building’s large atrium into “part F&B, part wellness”. Refurbishment is expected to take about 18 months.

The building sits on a 99-year lease from May 15, 1993, with about 66 years remaining. It is opposite City Developments’ Union Square, a 735,500 sq ft mixed-use redevelopment of the former Central Mall and Central Square , due for completion in 2029.

Manchharam sees Merchant House as a different proposition from Stamford Place. While Stamford Place is an integrated mixed-use development, Merchant House will be part of a larger mixed-use precinct anchored by Union Square.

Human scale

Elevate Capital continues to hunt for properties priced below replacement cost. “After refurbishment, we are still at a good price point,” says Manchharam.

Its sweet spot is buildings with a gross floor area of 50,000 to 100,000 sq ft, such as Stamford Place, at about 78,190 sq ft, and Merchant House, at 71,111 sq ft. “We are looking at properties that are of a human scale,” he says.

He also sees room to grow the APT brand, focusing on properties with 50 to 150 rooms.

Singapore will remain Elevate Capital’s main focus, but the firm will be “more opportunistic” overseas. One market Manchharam is watching is Hong Kong, where he lived for three years, over a decade ago. “I feel like the market is coming back,” he says. “We can see an uptick in terms of demand for commercial space.”

For now, there is plenty to work with closer to home. Many buildings in Singapore are reaching the 20- to 30-year mark, when owners must decide whether to retrofit or tear down and rebuild, says Zarch’s Chan, who is a founding member of the Singapore chapter of Docomomo, an international non-profit that documents and conserves modern-movement architecture.

Some may choose to sell instead. This is where Manchharam sees opportunity. “There are a lot of older buildings out there that are undermanaged,” he says. “We are looking at what we could potentially do with these buildings, and how we can reposition them, instead of redeveloping.”

title: Savills bets on scale, automation to reach 100,000 managed units by 2030
article:
Managing a luxury condo is no longer just about keeping the lifts running, facilities well-maintained, gardens manicured and common areas clean.

Increasingly, concierge services are expected to match those of five-star hotels. “Residents expect white-glove service,” says Savills Singapore CEO Marcus Loo, and the pricier the home, the higher the bar.

Take the 54-unit, ultra-luxury Park Nova by Shun Tak Holdings, completed in 2024, which Savills manages. In January 2025, the developer sold its largest penthouse, a 5,899 sq ft five-bedroom unit, for $38.888 million ($6,593 psf). Based on caveats lodged, that is the second-highest psf price ever paid for a condo unit in Singapore.

Residents paying such prices expect service to match. “They want best-in-class, uniformed staff — those who have excellent customer service, preferably former Singapore Airlines stewardesses who can communicate well and have technical know-how,” says Loo. “It’s very difficult to find a single individual with such qualities.”

At large suburban estates, the challenges are different. Savills was recently appointed managing agent of the 2,203-unit Treasure at Tampines , Singapore’s largest private condo by number of units.

Managing a development of that scale inevitably generates a high volume of feedback from residents, on everything from maintenance issues to landscaping, says Loo. The managing agent, he adds, needs both “technical know-how” and “service excellence.”

Whether in luxury or mass-market estates, residents now expect more from their managing agents. That adds to the pressure on an industry already grappling with one of its biggest challenges: finding and retaining experienced staff amid rising labour costs.

Building scale, bringing services in-house

For Savills, the response has been to build scale, bring more building services in-house, and increasingly deploy technology and robotics as it works towards a target of 100,000 strata units under management by 2030.

It currently manages 71,793 units across 226 strata developments, or 249 projects including non-strata properties.

The portfolio has more than doubled since August 2011, when Savills acquired a 51% stake in CKH Asset Management. At the time, the Singapore-based property management firm had 300 employees and managed close to 30,000 units across about 100 strata developments, primarily condos, as well as retail, office and industrial assets.

More recently, in September 2022, Savills Singapore acquired Absolute Maintenance Services, adding cleaning as well as mechanical and electrical (M&E) capabilities to its property management platform.

Savills further expanded its property and integrated facilities management (IFM) business in December 2025 by acquiring a 70% stake in Alpina Holdings, with an option to take full ownership in 2030.

Alpina provides building services, M&E, and alteration and addition works, mainly for government and public-sector clients.

The rationale is that more clients, including government agencies, are moving towards IFM, where a single provider takes responsibility for multiple building services.

Increasingly, clients prefer to appoint a single IFM company, says Loo. “They ideally do not wish to deal with multiple contractors — the M &E, cleaning services or the landscape companies.”

Bringing these functions in-house, rather than coordinating multiple external contractors, could eventually allow Savills to capitalise on economies of scale. Each estate would keep a leaner on-site team, supported by roving teams deployed across clusters of nearby developments.

Running a sizeable portfolio also requires back-office support and a manpower pool deep enough to deploy staff when needed, not just property managers on the ground, Loo adds.

Low barriers to entry fuel competition

Most managing agents are appointed for one to three years, and Loo estimates that, at any given time, about half of management councils are looking to switch. That churn keeps Savills busy. “We participate in almost 20 tenders every month,” he says.

Barriers to entry are also low. “There are a lot of new property management companies who break into the market by slashing prices despite the fact that they are making a loss,” says Loo. “That is not sustainable and, ultimately, it is the estate that loses.” Some estates that left Savills for cheaper rivals have since returned, he adds.

The potential market is substantial. According to Building and Construction Authority data published on data.gov.sg, there were 3,806 active Management Corporation Strata Title (MCST) developments across residential, commercial, mixed-use and industrial properties as at April 6.

Savills is betting that its in-house capabilities will give it an edge. “We offer our clients a one-stop-shop solution to manage key MCST services at lower cost to the estate due to economies of scale,” says Loo.

Rising costs drive automation

Costs are a pressure point for MCSTs. Loo estimates that property management costs have increased by more than 20% since the Covid-19 pandemic, driven by higher wages and foreign worker levies.

Winnie Wong, Savills Singapore senior managing director of property management, points to a broader set of pressures facing the sector, including increasingly complex regulatory requirements, higher operating and maintenance costs, and the challenges associated with ageing developments.

Addressing these issues will require both greater digitalisation and continued investment in workforce development, she says. That includes upskilling property management professionals and making the industry more attractive as a career.

For Loo, greater automation is inevitable. Cleaning and M&E services are the two largest cost components in managing an estate, followed by security and landscaping, he says.

Attitudes towards robot cleaners have also shifted. About five years ago, council members were wary of robotics, fearing the machines would not meet cleaning standards, says Loo. “So they still preferred the cleaning company to provide physical labour.”

Today, Absolute Maintenance Services is running demonstrations of robot cleaners at several estates. There are limits, however. “The thing about robot cleaners is that they need level ground,” he says. “The challenge with a lot of the estates is that they generally do not have flat surfaces.”

The machines are therefore deployed mainly in lobbies and common areas of apartment blocks, where they can clean at regular intervals around the clock. This has helped some councils cut manpower costs, Loo adds.

Automation is also changing how estates manage access. QR codes and facial recognition allow visitors and vehicles to enter and exit more smoothly.

Ageing estates: En bloc versus rising upkeep costs

On Sept 8, Parliament passed the Land Titles (Strata) (Amendment) Bill 2026, introducing a tiered reduction in collective-sale consent thresholds based on building age, and stricter procedural safeguards.

Under the changes, the consent threshold will be lowered to 70% from 80% for developments aged 40 to 59 years, and to 65% for those aged 60 years and above. It remains at 80% for developments aged more than 10 to 39 years, and at 90% for those 10 years or newer.

“I think in the next six to 12 months, because of this announcement, there may be a knee-jerk reaction by some of these estates who are trying to explore a collective sale,” says Loo. Savills has already received several enquiries from estates wanting to assess whether a sale makes sense. But Loo is unsure whether it will lead to a surge in en bloc sales.

There are a few factors at play. One is the Government Land Sales (GLS) Programme, which continues to offer developers a steady pipeline of sites. “They have many options in terms of GLS sites,” he says.

With that alternative, an en bloc site must offer enough upside to justify the extra cost. “The main reason developers would buy an old estate en bloc, pay for demolition costs and other additional costs, is that they can increase the number of units in the development, from 300 to 600, for example, or up to 1,000 units.”

Savills has first-hand experience managing older strata developments that have explored or completed collective sales. It has managed Roxy Square since July 1995. The freehold mixed-use development in Katong was put up for collective sale at $1.25 billion in 2024 and relaunched at a reduced $1.115 billion in 2025.

Loo says long-standing property management relationships can also generate referrals within Savills when a development begins exploring a collective sale.

For instance, Savills’ investment sales team handled the collective sales of two long-standing management clients: Delfi Orchard , sold to City Developments for $439 million in May 2024; and Concorde Hotel & Shopping Centre, acquired by Hotel Properties for $821 million in November that year. Savills had managed both since October 1995.

Meanwhile, for owners who stay put, maintaining an ageing condo can become increasingly expensive. Loo says major components such as lifts may need to be upgraded or modernised when developments reach their 20th to 25th year, failing which they become more prone to breakdowns.

But if an estate defers upgrades and cuts maintenance spending, upkeep suffers. Over time, Loo argues, that can affect not only the development’s image but also its value.

“If you want to stay in a condo, you must be prepared to pay to ensure the upkeep of the estate,” he says. “If there's a failure to maintain the estate, it inevitably affects the value of your property, and ultimately, the residents suffer."

title: CHINA 2040: Who Are DBS’ 14 Long-Term Champions?
article:
Even as China may grow much more slowly over the next 15 years, s

everal big investment themes could create hugely valuable companies.
DBS Research's new 265-page
China 2040: The Next Chapter of Innovation-Led Growth
report says:

DBS Research's new 265-page
China 2040: The Next Chapter of Innovation-Led Growth
report says:

"Compelling investment themes are emerging alongside the sectors driving China’s long-term growth."

China is expected to rely less on imported AI chips and build more of its own semiconductor ecosystem.
This should benefit local AI chipmakers and related suppliers. AI itself should also become deeply embedded in business operations. Large cloud and technology platforms could capture much of this value.
Advanced manufacturing will be another major growth area, especially
robotics, automation, precision components and the low-altitude economy
, such as drones and eVTOL aircraft.
Finally, China’s green transition will remain important.
By 2040, DBS expects electric vehicles to account for more than 90% of new-car sales, while advanced autonomous driving could become widespread. This should drive strong growth in
battery storage and renewable energy

.

How did DBS pick its Champions?

How did DBS pick its Champions?

How did DBS pick its Champions?

How did DBS pick its Champions?

DBS constructed a Seven-Pillar Framework, assessing companies on policy alignment, growth trajectory, moat durability, capital efficiency, geopolitical resilience, optionality and execution capacity.

So, it isn't simply chasing the companies with the fastest projected revenue growth.

Moat durability gets the largest weighting at 20%, followed by policy alignment at 18% and growth trajectory at 17%.

DBS explains why:

“Long-term compounding depends on defensible advantage, not sector growth alone.”

The 3 highest-ranked listed companies are
CATL, BeOne Medicines and Alibaba
.

Here's why

1. CATL: Batteries — but increasingly not just EV batteries

CATL (3750 HK) sits at the top with

DBS describing its investment case as an “unshakable market position underpinned by R&D leadership.”

CATL has ranked first globally in EV batteries for nine consecutive years and in energy-storage batteries for five.

DBS expects booming storage requirements from renewable energy, grid upgrades and AI data centres.
It estimates CATL's EV battery volumes could grow 17% annually through 2040, while energy-storage battery volumes grow even faster at 25%.

CATL also enjoys scale, strong R&D, broad patent protection and higher profitability than many competitors.

The catch is geopolitics. Tariffs and localisation rules may require more manufacturing outside China, raising costs.

2. BeOne Medicines: China's biotech goes global

BeOne Medicines (6160 HK) offers an entirely different route into China's innovation story.

Its attraction is what DBS calls a “China-cost/global-revenue structure.”

Much of BeOne's clinical development remains anchored in China, where DBS estimates trials cost 30–40% less than in the US and Europe.
Yet BeOne has built its own commercial operation across the US, Europe and more than 70 countries rather than simply licensing its drugs to Western pharmaceutical companies.

That potentially allows it to combine Chinese R&D economics with Western-market revenues.

It is also better insulated from US-China tensions than many Chinese biotech peers: BeOne has US manufacturing and derives more than half its revenue from the US.

The risks are familiar — clinical failures, regulatory setbacks and the possibility that today's promising pipeline doesn't deliver tomorrow's blockbuster drugs.

3. Alibaba: Can AI become the new profit engine?

Alibaba (9988 HK) is perhaps the most familiar name — but DBS's thesis is increasingly not about e-commerce.

DBS calls Alibaba:

“the clearest listed company through which to monetise AI” in China.

Alibaba combines its own chips, cloud infrastructure, Qwen AI models, enterprise distribution and real-world applications.

And crucially, it already has a cash-generating business capable of funding the enormous investment AI requires.

DBS expects Cloud and AI, just 13% of Alibaba revenue in 2025, to reach
52% by 2040
, with cloud overtaking core commerce around 2030.

The risks are intense AI competition, heavy capital spending and continuing regulatory pressures on the consumer-platform business.
DBS itself notes that “policy points in two directions” — supportive towards AI and domestic silicon, but more restrictive towards consumer platforms.

operate in completely different industries.

What connects them is scale, technology, financial resources, defensible competitive advantages and exposure to long-duration structural growth.

title: Far East Orchard JV acquires London freehold site for PBSA development
article:
Far East Orchard, through its joint venture company (JVCo), has acquired a freehold development site at 325 Borough High Street, Southwark, London, for GBP60 million ($102 million). The group intends to develop the site into a 444-bed purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA), targeted for completion by 2029.

A sale and purchase agreement (SPA) was entered into by Far East Orchard’s subsidiary, Borough High Street Development Limited and LDC (Portfolio) Limited on Sept 24.

Far East UK Student Accommodation Development Fund (FESAD), Far East Orchard’s UK PBSA development fund, holds an 85% interest in Borough High Street Development Limited through Far East PBSA Venture I Pte. Ltd. (FEPV). The remaining interests are held equally by Far East Orchard Investments (UK) Pte Ltd (FEOIUK) and Aurum Investments (Private) Limited, with 7.5% stakes each. FEPV and FEOIUK are wholly-owned subsidiaries of Far East Orchard. Aurum Investments is wholly-owned by Woh Hup Holdings.

This is the group’s third acquisition and first development in London. The purchase will expand its portfolio across London, Manchester and Glasgow comprising 956 PBSA beds. The acquisition will also bring the group’s PBSA portfolio to over 60,000 beds owned and managed.

“King’s Place marks a significant milestone for FESAD as our first development in London and the full deployment of the fund’s committed capital,” says Alan Tang, group CEO of Far East Orchard. “London remains one of the UK’s most attractive and supply-constrained student accommodation markets.”

“The acquisition will expand its development portfolio across three major UK cities. The development also demonstrates the strength of our integrated lodging platform, bringing together our investment, fund management, development, asset management and operating capabilities,” he adds.

See also: Centurion Corp acquires dormitory at Pasir Gudang for $67.2 mil

The site is located in London Zone 1 and is located close to several Russell Group universities including King’s College London, the London School of Economics and Political Science, Queen Mary University of London and Imperial College London. The site is also a four-minute walk from Borough Underground station and an eight-minute walk from Elephant & Castle station.

The development has received Gateway 2 approval, a milestone that allows construction to commence. Construction is targeted to begin in 4Q2026.

title: Bonds stabilise as oil declines, stocks edge up
article:
(Sept 25): A global bond sell-off that drove yields to multi-decade highs began to stabilise in Asia as oil snapped a two-day surge, offering investors some respite after a bruising stretch for debt markets.

Yields on the 10-year Treasury fell one basis point to 5.19%, easing after rallying more than 20 basis points in the past two sessions. Yields on the rate-sensitive two-year note declined by two basis points to 4.91%.

Providing support was a 0.7% drop in Brent to about US$105.90 a barrel Friday after a more than 7% rally in the past two sessions. The relief came as US and Iranian negotiators explored a phased deal that would see Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lift its blockade of Iranian ports. Elsewhere, gold advanced.

As sentiment stabilised, Asian stocks posted a modest advance and US equity-index futures pared earlier losses. MSCI’s Asia Pacific equities gauge climbed 0.2%, with eight of its 11 subgroups advancing. Gains largely came from Japan, as markets in South Korea, Taiwan and mainland China were closed for a holiday.

Oil prices and bond yields are likely to remain key drivers for markets, with still elevated energy costs adding to inflation pressures and reinforcing expectations for further Federal Reserve tightening. Swaps fully price three additional quarter-point hikes over the next year, a prospect that has driven long-term Treasury yields to multi-decade highs and increased pressure on equity valuations.

“Things will likely be a bit bumpy in the near term, in the run-up to the US midterm elections as a function of the politics, as a function of rates and also higher energy prices and greater geopolitical risks,” Timothy Moe, the chief APAC regional equity strategist at Goldman Sachs Group Inc, said on Bloomberg TV. “After that we think there is a clear roadmap towards a rally at the back end of the year, really propelled by earnings and attractive valuations.”

See also: Bond sell-off deepens as Fed rate-hike bets build

The global bond sell-off had extended into Asia as elevated oil prices stoked inflation concerns, pushing long-term Treasury yields to multi-decade highs and fuelling expectations for further interest-rate hikes by the Fed.

Australian and New Zealand 10-year bond yields advanced three basis points apiece, while the yield on a global bond index hit 4% for the first time since 2007. Japanese government debt also fell.

Moves in Asia Pacific tracked a global slump in bonds that pushed the 30-year Treasury yield to the highest since 2004 and lifted the 10-year yield eight basis points to 5.20% in the New York session.

See also: Asian stocks rise after US tech rally, oil drops

A Bloomberg gauge of the dollar held its gains from the previous session, trading around levels last seen in July. Gold edged higher to trade at about US$4,300 an ounce.

In Japan, yen intervention risk was back in focus as a two-week-long slide in the currency put it back within reach of the closely watched level of 160 per dollar. The currency traded slightly stronger at 158.70 in early Friday trading.

Strategists see the 160-per-dollar level emerging again as a test of Japan’s tolerance for yen weakness given its continued depreciation in the wake of the central bank’s policy meeting on Sept 18.

Attention remained firmly on bonds. The latest rise in yields extended a sharp repricing since the start of the US-Iran war.

Two-year Treasury yields have climbed more than 150 basis points over that period, while 30-year yields are up more than 80 basis points. Wednesday’s bond sell-off was among the biggest one-day drops since US President Donald Trump’s April 2025 tariff rollout.

“We are firmly set up for higher yields in this environment,” said Byron Anderson at Laffer Tengler Investments. “Rate hikes do not solve Iran, oil, the AI boom, or inflation. They do increase borrowing costs for everyone else in the market, which will eventually hit labour and the consumer if the Fed gets aggressive.”

title: Meta’s best month since 2013 has it on cusp of US$2 tril level
article:
(Sept 25): Meta Platforms Inc is finally seeing the stock breakout that beleaguered bulls had been banking on.

The Facebook parent’s shares have jumped 36% in September following the release of its Muse personal artificial intelligence (AI) assistant, which has risen quickly to the top of app charts and muffled concerns that heavy spending on AI won’t pay off. The stock is on pace for its best month since July 2013 and a roughly 1% gain away from joining an elite group of companies worth at least US$2 trillion ($2.56 trillion).

“Muse clearly validates its AI strategy and position, after a year and a half where the stock was basically flat because people didn’t know if AI was going to be a net positive or a net negative,” said Rob Biederman, co-founder and managing partner at Asymmetric Capital Partners. “It’s logical that AI agents will become the front door to the internet for a lot of people, which puts the balance of power in Meta’s favour,” he added.

This month’s rally has marked a dramatic reversal for Meta, whose shares struggled for much of the year amid doubts about its costly AI efforts and legal risks stemming from lawsuits targeting its social-media business. Less than six weeks ago, Meta shares were down 18% for the year in the wake of a disappointing revenue forecast in late July, putting the stock among the 50 worst performers in the S&P 500 through Aug 18.

Since then, however, Meta is the third-best performer in the benchmark with a 43% gain. The recovery began after Meta agreed late last month to pay as much as US$18 billion to settle a social-media lawsuit, removing a major overhang for the stock. But the biggest factor is excitement about new AI products and the potential revenue lift they could bring, which is giving investors like Biederman optimism that Meta shares have room to run.

See also: Qualcomm renews licensing pact with Apple starting in 2027

In a sign of how impressed investors are with Muse, they’ve been dumping the shares of companies in a broad range of industries over fears about potential disruption, similar to selloffs earlier this year sparked by AI startup Anthropic.

Already, Meta has announced a grocery-selling partnership with Instacart owner Maplebear Inc, as well as one with online travel agency Expedia Inc. At an event on Wednesday, Meta unveiled a number of products that analysts praised, including a palm-sized gadget for using Muse, as well as camera-free versions of its smart-glasses lineup.

“There’s still meaningful upside potential as Meta is in the early stages of releasing frontier models and AI-driven products beyond advertising,” JPMorgan analyst Doug Anmuth wrote in a Sept 10 note raising his rating on the stock to overweight from neutral.

See also: Oracle cites ‘force majeure’ to shield itself on controversial data centre — Bloomberg

Of course, Meta still has a long way to go to proving it can make enough money from its AI efforts to justify the vast expense. Capital spending is expected to be nearly US$140 billion this year, double the roughly US$70 billion Meta spent in 2025. That figure is expected to swell to US$197 billion next year and US$215 billion in 2028.

The heavy spending is taking a toll. After generating US$46 billion in free cash flow last year, Meta is expected to have negative free cash flow of US$6.4 billion in 2026, and negative US$29.2 billion next year.

That’s putting pressure on the company to deliver growth. Sales are expected to rise 26% to US$254 billion in 2026 while net income is expected to expand 33% to US$80.6 billion, according to the average of analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg. However, revenue and profit growth is expected to slow next year to 20% and 9%, respectively.

Meta is priced at 21 times profit expected over the next 12 months, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. While that’s up significantly from a June low of less than 14 times, it’s roughly the average multiple the stock has traded at over the past three years and a slight discount to the Nasdaq 100 at 22 times.

“Right now Meta offers a below-market multiple for above-market growth, which is attractive on its own, but it also has massive scale and distribution, which are advantages that will be really hard for competitors to overwhelm,” Biederman said.

Wall Street remains widely positive on Meta with more than 90% of the analysts tracked by Bloomberg rating the stock a buy. But the shares are trading around the average price target, suggesting upside could be limited over the next 12 months.

Given the extent of the rally, Meta shares are vulnerable to a pullback considering how fast perceptions can change in the market for AI services, according to Brandon Pizzurro, who helps oversee US$29 billion in assets as chief investment officer at GuideStone Funds.

“Sentiment on the big players seems to change as often as new AI models get released, and something like Muse gives markets the sugar rush of a new catalyst, but there’s an increasingly high bar to impress investors, and rightful trepidation on whether these companies can deliver,” Pizzurro said.

title: Crypto exchange Bitget halts withdrawals after US$352 mil hack
article:
(Sept 25): Crypto exchange Bitget reported an estimated US$351.6 million in unauthorised transfers from some of its wallets and temporarily suspended withdrawals.

“User funds are safe,” chief executive Gracy Chen said in a post on X early Friday in Singapore. “The full amount of this loss falls within the coverage of Bitget’s User Protection Fund, which currently holds over US$464 million.”

The hack continues a spate of recent attacks that have put crypto cybersecurity in the spotlight. Earlier this month, US$320 million worth of Bitcoin was drained from a wallet used by Liquid Network, while in August, the hack of the popular offline Bitcoin wallet Coldcard raised questions about the safest way to store the digital asset.

Chen said Bitget operates a three-tier wallet architecture and the breach was confined to portions of hot-wallet and warm-wallet layers, with cold wallets remaining secure.

“Deposits and trading remain fully operational,” she said. “Withdrawals are temporarily paused and will be restored as soon as the security review is complete.”

A full incident report including root cause analysis and corrective actions will be published within 24 hours, Chen said.

See also: Bitcoin bulls eye next leg as US$15 bil options expiry nears

“We will not speculate on the attack vector until the investigation is complete,” she added.

title: MGM Resorts is discussing making a bid for People, WSJ reports
article:
(Sept 25): MGM Resorts International is discussing making a bid to purchase Barry Diller’s People Inc, which owns a roughly 27% stake in MGM, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The news comes after People withdrew its own bid on Wednesday to buy the rest of the casino and resort company.

People, which owns its namesake magazine as well as other publications, has a market value of about US$2.7 billion. Diller had said in a statement on Wednesday that while his deal for MGM didn’t materialise, he was open to other possible transactions.

A spokesperson for the longtime entertainment and technology executive declined to comment.

title: Oil steadies with the US, Iran said to be exploring phased deal
article:
(Sept 25): Oil steadied as US and Iranian negotiators were said to be exploring a phased deal that would see Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

West Texas Intermediate for November was little changed above US$94 a barrel, after gaining almost 3% on Thursday, while Brent settled above US$106. The two countries — which have both refused to make similar deals in recent months — were pushing for a breakthrough on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, according to a person familiar with the discussions.

Crude has had another volatile week of trading, as the conflict between Washington and Tehran nears the end of its seventh month. Prices have been buffeted by mixed signals on the outlook for the war, signs of a pick-up in Middle East flows, and speculation the US may ban diesel exports. For the year, oil remains more than 60% higher, stoking global inflationary pressures.

Hormuz — the narrow waterway that links the Persian Gulf to global markets — has been at the center of the war between Washington and Tehran. The Islamic Republic has insisted that it has sovereign control over the conduit, which in peacetime used to carry about a fifth of daily global oil and natural gas supplies. The US has said the status of the route must not be changed, while also imposing a full naval blockade of Iran’s ports.

WTI for November traded 0.2% lower at US$94.45 a barrel at 6:02 a.m.

title: US stocks waver as oil rally triggers bond volatility
article:
(Sept 25): A renewed episode of bond volatility left traders reluctant to make riskier bets, with stocks wavering on worries that elevated oil prices will fuel inflation and force the Federal Reserve (Fed) to lift rates.

As the selloff in bonds deepened, 30-year yields hit the highest since 2004. The Treasury’s expanded buyback operation failed to live up to expectations. While the S&P 500 was little changed, most of its firms fell. Brent crude settled near US$107 after briefly paring its rally on news reports that the US and Iran are exploring a phased deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Investors are demanding greater compensation to hold bonds as concerns about persistent inflation, government spending and surging corporate borrowing to finance the artificial-intelligence buildout intensify. Against this backdrop, money markets now fully reflect three Fed hikes over the next year.

“We are firmly set up for higher yields in this environment,” said Byron Anderson at Laffer Tengler Investments. “Rate hikes do not solve Iran, oil, the AI boom, or inflation. They do increase borrowing costs for everyone else in the market, which will eventually hit labor and the consumer if the Fed gets aggressive.”

Meantime, President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping addressed their intense competition over AI on Thursday during a summit. Hours earlier, the US announced an agreement to extend its trade truce with China by around two months to Jan 10.

Traders also parsed comments from central bank officials. Fed Bank of Philadelphia president Anna Paulson joined the chorus of policymakers saying additional hikes may be needed to ensure inflation returns to their goal. Her New York colleague John Williams noted the Fed still has “a lot of work to do” in dealing with price pressures.

See also: US stocks fall as inflation jitters boost bond yields

Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack said the economy is facing a series of supply shocks, increasing the potential for an inflationary mindset to take hold. Her Richmond counterpart Tom Barkin noted a broad range of persistent cost pressures has raised the risk that inflation could become entrenched.

“While solid economic growth and healthy corporate fundamentals suggest interest rates are not yet restrictive enough to derail the expansion, the rapid increase in yields and elevated bond market volatility are creating a more meaningful headwind for equities,” said Angelo Kourkafas at Edward Jones.

Any easing of geopolitical tensions that helps relieve pressure on energy prices could go a long way toward stabilizing the bond market, in his view. Until then, Kourkafas believes upward pressure on yields is likely to persist as expectations for additional Fed tightening remain elevated.

See also: Nasdaq 100 eyes peak, oil falls on US-Iran talks

“Rising yields and higher oil prices are testing market resilience, but strong economic momentum and broad-based earnings growth continue to serve as powerful sources of support,” he added.
